title: UNIT 7: COORDINATE GEOMETRY
notes:
✓ Coordinate Geometry → connects algebra and geometry using coordinates, equations, lines and curves.

✓ Cartesian plane → consists of the x-axis and y-axis, which are perpendicular and intersect at the origin (0,0).

✓ A point is represented by an ordered pair (x,y).

◆ The plane is divided into four quadrants.

title: 7.1 DISTANCE BETWEEN TWO POINTS
notes:
For two points P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂), the distance is obtained using the Pythagorean theorem.

✓ Distance formula:
d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]

✓ The distance is always positive or zero.

◆ Horizontal points:
d = |x₂ − x₁|

◆ Vertical points:
d = |y₂ − y₁|.

title: DISTANCE EXAMPLE
notes:
Example: Find the distance between A(2,1) and B(8,9).

d = √[(8−2)² + (9−1)²]
  = √(6² + 8²)
  = √100
  = 10 units.

title: 7.2 DIVISION OF A LINE SEGMENT
notes:
✓ A line segment can be divided into equal parts or into a given ratio.

Example: A 15 cm segment is divided in the ratio 2:1.

✓ Total parts = 2 + 1 = 3
✓ Each part = 15/3 = 5 cm

Therefore:
✓ First part = 2 × 5 = 10 cm
✓ Second part = 1 × 5 = 5 cm.

title: SECTION FORMULA
notes:
If R(x,y) divides P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂) internally in the ratio p:q, where PR:RQ = p:q, then:

✓ x = (px₂ + qx₁)/(p + q)
✓ y = (py₂ + qy₁)/(p + q)

Therefore:
✓ R = ((px₂ + qx₁)/(p+q), (py₂ + qy₁)/(p+q)).

Use the coordinates of the opposite endpoints with the corresponding ratio.

title: MIDPOINT FORMULA
notes:
✓ The midpoint is the point that divides a line segment into two equal parts.

For P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂):

✓ M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2)

Example: A(−1,−2), B(3,2)

M = ((−1+3)/2, (−2+2)/2)
  = (1,0).

title: 7.3 EQUATION OF A LINE
notes:
✓ A straight-line equation can be determined when the slope and a point are known, or when two points are known.

✓ Slope (gradient) measures the steepness of a line.

For P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂):

✓ m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁),  x₁ ≠ x₂.

✓ A positive slope means the line rises from left to right.

✓ A negative slope means it falls from left to right.
✓ A zero slope gives a horizontal line.
✓ A vertical line has no slope.

title: ANGLE OF INCLINATION
notes:
✓ The angle of inclination θ is the anticlockwise angle between the positive x-axis and a non-vertical line.

For a non-vertical line:

✓ m = tan θ

Therefore:
✓ θ = tan⁻¹(m), when an appropriate angle is required.

◆ Acute angle of inclination → positive slope.

◆ Obtuse angle of inclination → negative slope.

title: POINT-SLOPE FORM
notes:
If a line has slope m and passes through P(x₁,y₁), its point-slope equation is:

✓ 𝒚 − 𝒚₁ = 𝒎(𝒙 − 𝒙₁)

Example: A line with slope 2 passing through (5,4):

y − 4 = 2(x − 5)

y = 2x − 6.

title: SLOPE-INTERCEPT FORM
notes:
✓ The slope-intercept form is:

𝒚 = 𝒎𝒙 + 𝒃

m → slope
b → y-intercept

Example:
y = 2x + 2

Here:
✓ Slope = 2
✓ Y-intercept = 2.

title: TWO-POINT FORM
notes:
For a line passing through P₁(x₁,y₁) and P₂(x₂,y₂):

✓ 𝒚 − 𝒚₁ = [(𝒚₂ − 𝒚₁)/(𝒙₂ − 𝒙₁)](𝒙 − 𝒙₁)

✓ This form is useful when two points on a line are given.

First calculate the slope:
✓ m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)

Then substitute into the point-slope equation.

title: GENERAL EQUATION OF A LINE
notes:
✓ The general form of a straight line is:

𝑨𝒙 + 𝑩𝒚 + 𝑪 = 𝟎

where A, B and C are real numbers.

Example:
5x + 2y + 10 = 0

To find the slope, rearrange into y = mx + b form when possible.

title: INTERCEPT FORM
notes:
✓ If a line has x-intercept p and y-intercept q, where p and q are non-zero, its equation is:

x/p + y/q = 1.

✓ x-intercept → point where the line crosses the x-axis.

✓ y-intercept → point where the line crosses the y-axis.

title: 7.4 PARALLEL LINES
notes:
✓ Two non-vertical lines are parallel when they have the same slope.

If slopes are m₁ and m₂:

✓ m₁ = m₂

Example:
Line 1: y = 2x + 1
Line 2: y = 2x − 6

Both have slope 2, so they are parallel.

✓ Parallel lines do not meet.

title: PERPENDICULAR LINES
notes:
✓ Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular if the product of their slopes is −1.

✓ 𝒎₁ × 𝒎₂ = −𝟏

Therefore:
✓ m₂ = −1/m₁

Example:
If m₁ = 2,
then m₂ = −1/2.

Thus a line with slope 2 is perpendicular to a line with slope −1/2.

title: PARALLEL/PERPENDICULAR EXAMPLE
notes:
Find the equation of the line through (5,4) parallel to y = 2x + 1.

Given slope = 2.

Using point-slope form:
y − 4 = 2(x − 5)

y = 2x − 6.

For a perpendicular line:
✓ Slope = −1/2

y − 4 = −1/2(x − 5)

y = −1/2x + 13/2.

title: 7.5 EQUATION OF A CIRCLE
notes:
✓ A circle in coordinate geometry is the set of all points that are at a fixed distance from a fixed center.

✓ Standard equation:

(𝒙 − 𝒉)² + (𝒚 − 𝒌)² = 𝒓²

(h,k) → center
r → radius.

✓ This equation represents all points on the circumference of the circle.

title: CIRCLE WITH CENTER AT ORIGIN
notes:
If the center is the origin (0,0), the standard equation becomes:

✓ 𝒙² + 𝒚² = 𝒓²

Example: A circle centered at the origin with radius 6:

x² + y² = 36.

title: CIRCLE EXAMPLE
notes:
Find the equation of a circle with center C(3,4) and radius 2.

Use:
(x−h)² + (y−k)² = r²

Therefore:
✓ (x−3)² + (y−4)² = 4.

title: CIRCLE THROUGH A GIVEN POINT
notes:
If the center (h,k) is known and the circle passes through P(x₁,y₁), first find the radius using the distance formula:

✓ r² = (x₁−h)² + (y₁−k)².

Then substitute r² into:

✓ (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r².

Example: Center (3,4), point (5,6):

r² = (5−3)² + (6−4)² = 8

Equation:
(x−3)² + (y−4)² = 8.

title: GENERAL EQUATION OF A CIRCLE
notes:
✓ The general equation of a circle is:

𝒙² + 𝒚² + 𝒍𝒙 + 𝒎𝒚 + 𝒏 = 𝟎

where l, m and n are real numbers.

To find the center and radius, use completing the square.

✓ Center:
(−l/2, −m/2)

✓ Radius:
r = 1/2√(l² + m² − 4n)

✓ For a real non-point circle:
l² + m² − 4n > 0.

title: COMPLETING THE SQUARE FOR A CIRCLE
notes:
Example:
x² + y² − 12x − 16y + 19 = 0

Group terms:
(x²−12x) + (y²−16y) = −19

Complete squares:
(x−6)² + (y−8)² = 81

Therefore:
✓ Center = (6,8)
✓ Radius = 9 units.

title: 7.6 AREA OF A TRIANGLE IN COORDINATE GEOMETRY
notes:
For a triangle with vertices:
(x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃),

✓ Area is:

A = 1/2 |x₁(y₂−y₃) + x₂(y₃−y₁) + x₃(y₁−y₂)|

✓ The absolute value ensures that the area is positive.

title: AREA EXAMPLE
notes:
Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(−3,4), B(0,1), C(−3,−2).

A = 1/2 |(−3)(1−(−2)) + 0(−2−4) + (−3)(4−1)|

= 1/2 |−9 + 0 − 9|

= 9 square units.

title: USING COORDINATES TO CLASSIFY TRIANGLES
notes:
✓ Coordinates can be used to determine the type of a triangle.

✓ Use the distance formula to compare side lengths.
✓ Use slopes to test perpendicular sides.

✓ If two sides have equal lengths → isosceles triangle.

✓ If m₁ × m₂ = −1 → the two sides are perpendicular → right angle.

✓ If all three side lengths are equal → equilateral triangle.

title: UNIT 7 QUICK FORMULA SHEET
notes:
◆ Distance:
✓ d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²]

◆ Midpoint:
✓ M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2)

◆ Section formula:
✓ R = ((px₂+qx₁)/(p+q), (py₂+qy₁)/(p+q))

◆ Slope:
✓ m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)

◆ Point-slope:
✓ y−y₁ = m(x−x₁)

◆ Slope-intercept:
✓ y = mx+b

◆ Two-point:
✓ y−y₁ = [(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)](x−x₁)

◆ General line:
✓ Ax + By + C = 0

◆ Parallel:
✓ m₁ = m₂

◆ Perpendicular:
✓ m₁m₂ = −1

◆ Circle:
✓ (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r²

◆ Circle at origin:
✓ x² + y² = r²

◆ General circle:
✓ x² + y² + lx + my + n = 0

◆ Triangle area:
✓ A = 1/2|x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)|.
